newsitem.title: USA: Currencies in line with fundamentals now - IMF.
newsitem.headline: Currencies in line with fundamentals now - IMF.

text.p: Exchange rates of major currencies appear now to be about in line with fundamentals, although the dollar may have risen a bit too far against the yen from a medium-term perspective, the IMF said on Wednesday.

"Exchange rates of the major currencies appear to be reasonably consistent with fundamentals, taking into account cyclical conditions," the International Monetary Fund said in its semi-annual World Economic Outlook.

The strength of the dollar and sterling is helping to restrain inflation in the United States and the United Kingdom, respectively, while the fragile economic recoveries in Japan., Germany and France are being supported by the weakness of those countries' currencies, it said.
Nevertheless, the IMF said that some of the recent rise of the dollar against the Japanese yen may not be beneficial in the medium run.
"Over the medium term, some of the recent appreciation of the dollar and depreciation of the yen may not be compatible with further reduction of external imbalances," it said.
IMF chief economist Michael Mussa told reporters in a briefing that a further fall of the yen at this time would not be welcome, but would not be a matter for "intense concern."

The IMF is forecasting that Japan's current account surplus will widen to $78 billion this year and $90 billion in 1998, from $66 billion last year. The U.S. deficit is expected to widen to $187 billion this year and $200 billion in 1998 from $165 billion last year.
"Some widening of the Japanese current account surplus should be anticipated and is not undesirable from a broader world perspective," Mussa told Reuters Financial Television.
At his briefing for reporters, Mussa said he expects to see both the Japanese yen and the German mark rise over the next two to there years as the economies of those two countries recover.
The dollar is currently trading at about 126 yen and 1.71 marks.
Mussa told Reuters Financial Television that the current dollar/mark level was not an immediate source of worry.
He said a rise of the dollar to 1.80 marks was "certainly feasible and possible" and would spark "a little more concern that too much of a good thing ceases to be a good thing."
Analysts said that the dollar's continued buoyancy on world currency markets partly reflects interest rate differentials.
Noting that the financial markets generally expect a further half percentage point rise in U.S. short-term interest over the course of this year, Mussa said, "That would accord with my judgement."

But he hastened to say that does not mean that the Federal Reserve will necessarily raise rates at its next meeting on May 20, adding that much will depend on the economic data that come out between now and then.
His perception though is that the underlying pace of the U.S. expansion remains a little bit faster than its long-run potential, making higher interest rates necessary eventually.
